extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and policymakers (late 18th century readers of Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political pamphlet reflecting on the French Revolution, arguing for the preservation of traditional manners, institutions, and religion while critiquing radical Enlightenment doctrines and revolutionary methods. The text offers principles for judging political change and for preserving social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of chivalry, manners, and traditional honor
rubrics_metrics.description: This mixed system of opinion and sentiment had its origin in the ancient chivalry ... It was this which has given its character to modern Europe. It produced a noble equality and handed it down through all gradations of social life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that chivalric sensibilities—loyalty to rank and sex, dignified obedience, submission, and the 'chastity of honor'—softened power, ennobled individuals, mitigated vice, and served as the 'nurse of manly sentiment and heroic enterprise.' Losing these manners would be a grave loss to civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affections and manners as necessary supplements to law
rubrics_metrics.description: These public affections, combined with manners, are required sometimes as supplements, sometimes as correctives, always as aids to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that laws alone cannot engender love, veneration, admiration, or attachment; affections and manners create social bonds that reason alone (which banishes affections) cannot replace. Institutions must be embodied in persons to inspire allegiance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of the 'conquering empire of light and reason' that strips social drapery
rubrics_metrics.description: All the decent drapery of life is to be rudely torn off. All the superadded ideas ... are to be exploded as a ridiculous, absurd, and antiquated fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that a mechanistic/philosophic approach which discards traditional 'drapery' will leave institutions supported only by terror and private interest, destroying the affectional basis of society and making institutions brittle and prone to tyranny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject justifying regicide or atrocity by utilitarian calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: On this scheme of things ... Regicide, and parricide, and sacrilege, are but fictions of superstition ... if the people are by any chance or in any way gainers by it, a sort of homicide much the most pardonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticizes the anti-moral calculus that weighs crimes against contingent advantages; shows by example that permitting such reasoning normalizes perfidy and murder, leading to systemic preference for criminal means and the erosion of moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve established institutions (church, monarchy, aristocracy, democracy) in their proper degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: We cleave closely to them. We are resolved to keep an established church, an established monarchy, an established aristocracy, and an established democracy, each in the degree it exists, and in no greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for conserving existing mixed constitution elements rather than radical alteration; institutions have moral and civil functions that cannot be safely discarded or replaced abruptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consecration of the state by a state religious establishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The consecration of the state by a state religious establishment is necessary ... that all who administer in the government of men ... should have high and worthy notions of their function and destination; that their hope should be full of immortality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religion connected to the state inculcates awe, accountability, and the sense of acting 'in trust' before a higher power; this moral framing restrains abuse and promotes dignified public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of nobility and clergy as protectors of learning and civilization
rubrics_metrics.description: The nobility and the clergy, the one by profession, and the other by patronage, kept learning in existence ... Learning paid back what it received to nobility and to priesthood, and paid it with usury, by enlarging their ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that arts, learning, and higher culture historically depended on and were fostered by established elites; removing their protective role risks debauchment of learning and cultural decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice (traditional prejudices) as a social good and habit-former
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice renders a man's virtue his habit, and not a series of unconnected acts. Through just prejudice, his duty becomes a part of his nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes 'just prejudice' from mere ignorance: traditional prejudices can supply motive and permanence to moral behavior, preventing paralysis of decision that pure reason might cause in emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism of philosophic cabals/freethinkers when they act as political factions
rubrics_metrics.description: A cabal, calling itself philosophic, receives the glory of many of the late proceedings ... With us they were and are wholly unconnected individuals. With us they kept the common nature of their kind, and were not gregarious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that intellectuals who band together as a political corps are dangerous because they substitute novel theory for earned institutions and act without the stabilizing sanctions of religion and tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of manners to commerce, trade, and the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even commerce, and trade, and manufacture ... certainly grew under the same shade in which learning flourished. They, too, may decay with their natural protecting principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that economic prosperity and the arts depend on the same cultural foundations (manners, religion, noble protection); attacking those foundations risks economic and artistic decline, producing a 'nation of gross, stupid, ferocious' people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice in punishing tyrants must be grave, decorous, and dignified
rubrics_metrics.description: The punishment of real tyrants is a noble and awful act of justice; and it has with truth been said to be consolatory to the human mind. But ... Justice is grave and decorous, and in its punishments rather seems to submit to a necessity than to make a choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condemns triumphal, vindictive displays (public insult and degrading triumph), advocating measured, dignified punishment that preserves justice's solemnity rather than satisfying brutal popular exultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discarding religion without presenting a replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: Before we take from our establishment the natural, human means of estimation, and give it up to contempt ... we desire that some other may be presented to us in the place of it. We shall then form our judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses concern that removing the established religion without offering a legitimate substitute will leave a void the mind cannot endure, likely to be filled by pernicious superstition or degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre as a school of moral sentiments superior to some churches
rubrics_metrics.description: Indeed, the theatre is a better school of moral sentiments than churches where the feelings of humanity are thus outraged. Poets ... would not dare to produce such a triumph as a matter of exultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the theatre as an example of popular moral education: audiences naturally reject Machiavellian maxims and are trained in sympathy and moral intuition in ways that abstract political sermons may not achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachment to country grounded in long-standing customs and sentiments, not fleeting reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Their attachment to their country itself is only so far as it agrees with some of their fleeting projects ... We preserve the whole of our feelings still native and entire, unsophisticated by pedantry and infidelity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts that patriotism rooted in inherited manners and religion is more stable and valuable than attachment based on transient theorizing or ephemeral political schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: When fealty and traditional principles vanish, power resorts to worse means
rubrics_metrics.description: When the old feudal and chivalrous spirit of fealty ... shall be extinct in the minds of men, plots and assassinations will be anticipated by preventive murder and preventive confiscation ... Kings will be tyrants from policy, when subjects are rebels from principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicts that removing honor-based restraints will cause the state to secure itself by preemptive cruelty and legalized violence rather than honor and consent, creating a more brutal political code.
